summary: This standards-track document defines the canonical syntax of Uniform Resource Names, which are meant to be persistent, location-independent identifiers for resources. It was replaced by RFC 8141.

eli5.summary: A name for a book that stays the same even if the book moves to a different shelf.

questions: what is a uniform resource name
what is a namespace identifier in a urn
how are urns compared for equality
which characters are reserved in a urn
subtitle: The fixed shape every Uniform Resource Name must have: urn, a namespace, and a name.

tldr.problem: Uniform Resource Names are meant to be persistent, location-independent identifiers, so many existing naming systems need one common, transcribable form to fit into.
tldr.mechanism: Every URN is written as urn:, a Namespace Identifier, a colon and a Namespace Specific String, using a limited character set with %-escapes for everything else.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2141 was replaced by RFC 8141, so new work should use that document instead.

facts.label: NID length
facts.value: 1 letter or digit plus 1 to 31 more

today: RFC 2141 is obsoleted by RFC 8141, which replaces this URN syntax specification.

sections.title: What a URN Is For
sections.content:
Uniform Resource Names (URNs) are intended to serve as persistent, location-independent resource identifiers. They are also designed to make it easy to map other namespaces that share those properties into URN-space.

Because of that, the URN syntax gives a way to encode character data so that it can be sent in existing protocols and transcribed on most keyboards.
sections.eli5: A URN is a name that says what something is, not where it lives. This memo says how to spell such names so they work everywhere.

sections.title: The Overall Syntax
sections.content:
Every URN has the form "urn:" <NID> ":" <NSS>. The NID is the Namespace Identifier and the NSS is the Namespace Specific String. The leading urn: is case-insensitive.

The NID decides how the NSS is interpreted syntactically. The RFC notes that RFC 1630 and RFC 1737 push toward limiting the syntax, while supporting legacy naming systems pushes toward broadening it, so the two parts are specified separately.

A NID is a letter or digit, optionally followed by 1 to 31 more letters, digits or hyphens. It is case-insensitive, so ISBN and isbn name the same namespace. The NID urn is reserved and MUST NOT be used, to avoid confusion with the urn: prefix.
sections.eli5: Every URN starts with the word urn, then the kind of name it is, then the name itself, like a label that says urn, book-number, and the number.

sections.title: Characters and %-Escapes
sections.content:
The NSS is one or more URN characters: letters, digits, a set of punctuation such as parentheses, plus, comma, hyphen, period, colon, equals, at, semicolon, dollar, underscore, exclamation mark, asterisk and apostrophe, or a % followed by two hex digits. Names that contain other characters MUST be translated into this canonical form before they are used as protocol elements. Each outside character is encoded as one to six octets using UTF-8, and each octet becomes % plus two hex digits.

Four characters are reserved: the percent sign, the slash, the question mark and the hash sign. The % introduces an escape, and a literal % in a namespace must be written %25. The other three are reserved for future developments, and namespace developers SHOULD NOT use them unencoded.

Some characters are explicitly excluded and MUST be %-encoded if used: octets 1 to 32, octets 127 to 255, and the backslash, double quote, ampersand, angle brackets, square brackets, caret, backtick, braces, vertical bar and tilde. Octet 0 should never be used, encoded or not. A URN ends when an excluded character is met, and that character is not part of the URN.
sections.eli5: Names may only use a safe set of letters and symbols. Anything unusual gets swapped for a percent sign and two letters or numbers, like writing a secret code for a funny character.

sections.title: Presentation, Legacy Names and URL Software
sections.content:
Any namespace that qualifies as a URN namespace MUST be expressed in this syntax, including existing legacy naming systems. All URN transport and interchange MUST use the canonical format. URN-aware applications MUST offer the option of showing URNs in canonical form so they can be copied directly, but MAY also show a friendlier form that replaces %-notation with extended characters.

The appendix covers URL software. A resolver that follows the URL syntax of the time will see a scheme of urn:, not urn:<nid>. It MUST treat a URN as an opaque URL and pass it, with the urn: tag, to a URN resolver. A browser SHOULD display the complete URN, including urn:, to avoid confusion between namespace identifiers and URL scheme identifiers.
sections.eli5: Every program has to pass names around in the plain, safe spelling. A program can show a prettier version to people, but must let them copy the real one.

sections.title: Deciding When Two URNs Match
sections.content:
Two URNs are lexically equivalent if they are octet-by-octet equal after three steps: normalize the case of the leading urn:, normalize the case of the NID, and normalize the case of any %-escaping. %-escaping MUST NOT be removed.

In the RFC's examples, URN:foo:a123,456, urn:foo:a123,456 and urn:FOO:a123,456 are equivalent, while urn:foo:A123,456 is not. urn:foo:a123%2C456 and URN:FOO:a123%2c456 are equivalent only to each other.

A namespace may add more equivalences, such as a case-insensitive NSS, but they must be documented at registration and may only remove false negatives. Functional equivalence is decided by each namespace's own practice and resolvers, and is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Two names count as the same if they only differ in capital letters in the fixed parts, like Urn and urn. Capitals in the name part can make a different name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document only specifies syntax. Namespace resolvers may give special meaning to some characters in the NSS, but any security concerns from that are outside its scope. The RFC strongly recommends that the namespace registration process include such considerations.
sections.eli5: This memo only says how to spell names. Any safety worries about a particular kind of name belong to whoever sets up that kind.
